summary: SL-059 closed live drift left over from SL-038: RigLock's mutex was documented and named as if it were machine-wide when it only ever serialised runs within one Windows sign-in session. The slice renamed the misleading constant (MachineName to SessionName, string value unchanged), fixed the three comments SL-038's own code review had flagged and left unfixed, and added an explicit per-session scope statement plus a documented trigger for a future Global\\ switch. It deliberately did not build a cross-session test, since a risk spike showed the only unattended route to a second Windows session is refused by this agent's own sandbox.

candidates.title: Fix the still-inaccurate curly-quote claim in WindowScriptParseTests.cs's class summary
candidates.why: code-review #4 and validate #5 both measured that curly quotes (U+2018/19/1C/1D) give errors=0 under PowerShell 5.1, not the 2 errors the shipped summary claims for 'a curly quote or dash'; only dashes give 2. It was filed as drift twice and shipped anyway.

candidates.title: Run the person-run SMB-LOOPBACK network test pass (WindowCases.ps1 -Case All -IncludeNetwork; Core.Tests Network=SMB-LOOPBACK)
candidates.why: validate-slice named this as not-reached in every one of its six attempts on this slice, and it was already not-reached on SL-038 before it. It never runs by engine (opt-in filter, excluded by default) and nobody has run it by hand across two slices now.

candidates.title: Reconcile design records' doc path 'docs/SL-020-scanner.md' with the real file 'docs/design/SL-020-scanner.md'
candidates.why: code-review flagged this exact mismatch on SL-038 and again on SL-059 (code-review #4 LEFT OPEN, 'still true from the earlier review'); it has now survived two full slices unfixed.

candidates.title: Engine fix: route an 'accepted-pending' code-review finding to build-slice before the next validate-slice run
candidates.why: O-007 was accepted-pending after code-review #1, but the pipeline went straight from code-review #2 to validate-slice #1 without the builder ever seeing it, per validate-slice #2's own account -- wasting a full validate cycle.

candidates.title: Cross-session RigLock exclusion (switch to Global\, prove exclusion in both creation orders by hand)
candidates.why: This design explicitly declined to build it, since the only unattended route to a second session is refused by the agent sandbox (spike 1, no-go). The trigger is now written into docs/design/SL-020-scanner.md for whenever a real cross-session need arises.

payload.estimate_error: Right on code scope (a rename plus three comment fixes, exactly what build-check called 'materially smaller than a fresh slice'), wrong on risk tier. Low risk skipped critique/critique-review, so the one real defect -- a class-summary claim about PowerShell 5.1 parsing behaviour that turned out to be factually wrong -- was never caught before code landed. It then took 3 build-slice attempts, 4 code-reviews and 6 validate-slice attempts to converge, and even the final shipped text is still partly wrong (curly quotes), accepted as drift rather than fixed. A slice whose deliverable includes a precise, falsifiable claim about environment behaviour needs an adversarial pass before build, regardless of how small the diff is.

learned.lesson: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (cp1252) only breaks parsing of a double-quoted string on em/en dash bytes (0x96/0x97, which map to 0x93/0x94 curly quotes territory is wrong here -- dashes only); curly quotes and accented letters parse fine there, and nothing non-ASCII breaks parsing inside a comment on either 5.1 or 7. Three separate attempts in this slice stated the general rule wrong before landing close to correct -- any future claim about this needs per-character measurement, not reasoning from 'non-ASCII breaks 5.1'.
learned.evidence: code-review #4 and validate #5/#3 measured em/en dash = 2 errors, curly quotes/apostrophe/e-acute = 0 errors, comments = 0 errors regardless, under real powershell.exe 5.1.26100.9444.

learned.lesson: An 'accepted-pending' code-review finding must route the slice back to build-slice before the next validate-slice runs; this loop let one run straight from code-review to validate-slice with the fix undone, which validate caught and had to send back itself.
learned.evidence: validate-slice #2's account: 'the pipeline went straight from review to validate, so the builder never saw it.'

learned.lesson: RigLock's kernel-object name string is decoupled from its C# identifier by design now (SessionName is just a label; the wire string stays Local\FsAnalyser-SmbRig). Any future rename of the identifier must not touch the string, since StallRig -- built outside FsAnalyser.slnx and invisible to `dotnet test FsAnalyser.slnx` -- opens it by that literal string and needs its own separate build to catch a missed rename.
learned.evidence: O-001/O-005 verification: StallRig built via its own csproj outside the slnx, reflection confirmed the string unchanged.

learned.lesson: The agent sandbox itself vetoes Register-ScheduledTask (even S4U/LogonType Limited) as a policy guard, independent of Windows account permissions. Any future slice needing a second Windows logon session cannot get one through this loop -- that question is settled, not worth re-spiking.
learned.evidence: risk-spike experiment 1: 'Register-ScheduledTask threw "Access is denied" under S4U/Limited' -- confirmed as the sandbox's own guard, not a Windows privilege error.

learned.lesson: Low risk tier (which skips critique/critique-review) is a poor fit whenever the deliverable includes a precise, checkable claim about environment behaviour (parser quirks, OS version differences) rather than just a code change -- those claims need adversarial review before build, not discovery through repeated code-review/validate cycles after the fact.
learned.evidence: code-review ran 4 times and validate-slice 6 times on a slice build-check itself sized as 'three doc-comment corrections,' almost entirely chasing the accuracy of one test class summary.

missed.what: code-review #3 passed the O-007 fix (a new WindowCasesIsAscii test plus a rewritten class summary) without checking that the rewritten summary was still factually accurate -- it still claimed the parse check 'covers code and string literals,' a claim the design's own send-back had already flagged as wrong. validate-slice #4 caught it instead and sent the slice back to build-slice for a third attempt.

payload.reason: Both alternative resolutions the drift item allowed (switch to Global\\, or correct the stale claims) were on the table; the correct-the-claims branch is now fully done and the Global\\ branch was explicitly declined after a spike showed it unautomatable in this sandbox, with the decision and its trigger written into the docs rather than left implicit.
payload.summary: SL-059 closed live drift left over from SL-038: RigLock's mutex was documented and named as if it were machine-wide when it only ever serialised runs within one Windows sign-in session. The slice renamed the misleading constant (MachineName to SessionName, string value unchanged), fixed the three comments SL-038's own code review had flagged and left unfixed, and added an explicit per-session scope statement plus a documented trigger for a future Global\\ switch. It deliberately did not build a cross-session test, since a risk spike showed the only unattended route to a second Windows session is refused by this agent's own sandbox.
unknowns: Does the SMB client's 'one port per server name' limit for 127.0.0.1 apply per logon session or machine-wide? If machine-wide, two rig runs in different sessions could still collide at the redirector even though RigLock itself would not serialise them.

Is an SMB mapping made in one sign-in session visible to Get-SmbMapping, and so to the rig's sweep, in another session (O-006)? This determines whether a per-session lock actually covers everything the sweep can touch, and needs a person with a second session to answer.
what_went_wrong: An 'accepted-pending' code-review finding (m1/O-007) was not routed to build-slice before the next validate-slice ran, so validate-slice #1/#2 had to discover and send back a fix the builder had never been shown.

code-review #3 passed the O-007 fix without verifying the rewritten class summary was factually accurate; validate-slice #4 caught the residual inaccuracy and sent the slice back for a third build attempt.

Even after that third fix, the shipped class summary still contains a measurably wrong claim about curly quotes (code-review #4 and validate #5 both found and re-confirmed it); it was accepted as non-blocking drift rather than corrected, so the slice closes with known-inaccurate prose in test code.

A single minor wording finding drove 2 extra build-slice attempts, 3 extra code-review attempts and up to 5 extra validate-slice attempts -- far more rework than a low-risk, no-critique slice was sized for.
